posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
This is basic accounting. When you have a bank deposit you hold an asset and the bank has a liability. Reserves are an asset for the bank and a liability of the Fed. But the Fed's liability is to the bank, not to you. You don't have a claim on reserves because they aren't your asset and they aren't the bank's liability to you. Your claim is on the bank, full stop.

You can't even hold reserves. Only banks and a handful of other institutions with Fed accounts can. When you send money to someone at another bank, your bank settles with their bank in reserves. Your deposit goes away and they get a new one, but the reserves never touch your hands.

The one time you end up holding a Fed liability is when you withdraw cash. Your bank swaps reserves for paper currency and hands it to you. That's a Fed liability, but it's a different one. It isn't reserves.

quoted.text:
On the eve of The AGI Chronicles (which comes out tomorrow!) I'm publishing an excerpt from "Big Blob of Compute," a 2017 internal research document by Dario Amodei, back when he was a researcher at OpenAI. 

It's never been published before, but BBOC is, in my mind, the essay that started the AI race. It described Amodei's hypothesis that scaling up AI models was the best way, by far, to make them smarter. GPT-2 was an experiment to test the hypothesis, and when it worked, OpenAI went all-in on scaling, which led to the race we have today.

It's a fascinating historical artifact that deserves to see the light of day. And it's taken on mythical proportions inside the AI industry, which is now spending trillions of dollars building the "big blobs" that Amodei thought would be necessary to get to AGI.

Enjoy! And please pre-order the book if you do! 

https://kevinroose.substack.com/p/the-essay-that-started-the-ai-race

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Today’s minutes: the FOMC already agrees on a December hike. The only disagreement is timing. Hiking before falling oil and gas prices show up, and before the data is even in? That’s a joke!

Governor Waller lost the argument for moving in October, so he took it to CNBC to “shock people” with 50bp.
He’s pre-committing to a jumbo hike weeks before the next round of data is in. Deciding before you’ve looked at the data isn’t vigilance. It’s malpractice.

Losing a debate in the room and relitigating it on TV is immature. It undercuts Chair Warsh and whipsaws markets for no policy gain.

This is not how the FOMC should act. It’s an embarrassment to everyone who works at the Fed. So much for a data-dependent, apolitical Fed.
Services inflation has run above 2% in 94.6% of months since 1968. Shock therapy won’t change that. Only a recession will.
